This supports considering both enablement and product work, but does not establish a firm threshold between them.

sections.heading: Product change versus enablement
sections.content: As a synthesis of her guidance: consider changing the product when customer feedback surfaces a recurring unmet need or product-level pain; enablement may be enough when customers mainly need to understand how to use an existing capability. Christine contrasts feedback that customers would benefit from a product offering with questions that amount to “teach me how to do this thing” (S1). For the latter, she describes customer education—including in-product content, technical documentation, and playbooks developed with product marketing—as ways to reduce friction and support engagement (S3). She recommends bringing together qualitative and quantitative customer inputs to understand the balance (S5). She does not give a formal cutoff for deciding between the two.

sections.heading: Product change versus enablement
sections.content: At Pendo, they looked at the quality and themes of inbound questions: were customers asking what the product does because they would benefit from it, or asking how to do something? The former can surface a product or value gap worth addressing; the latter may be addressed by enabling customers to use the existing product. Itwaru describes customer education, technical documentation for those who need more detail, and in-app playbooks developed with product marketing to reduce friction and drive engagement. The evidence gives this distinction and examples of enablement, but does not set out a stricter decision rule or guarantee that enablement alone will resolve friction.
